notes: The shared configuration objects: the blocks that appear inside MANY data/*.json records and are parsed once, in db_ops/lib, rather than by each app. This file is the field-level reference for them - what each field does, whether it is required, what values it accepts, and what its number is measured against.

Eleven entries: six objects (time_window, notify, notify_rule, output, cmd_access, sql_access), one shared FIELD (cleanup_retention) and four whole RECORDS (app_command, added 2026-09-21; backup_entry, backup_job and restore_entry, added 2026-09-22). 'field_count' and 'required_field_count' are stated per entry so a reader can see the shape before reading it. The four records carry kind 'field' deliberately - see their 'kind_note': that is the kind whose declared names the reader looks for directly ON the record, which is what a whole record is. backup_entry, backup_job and restore_entry are described separately although they live in ONE file, because they share only two field names (active, note) and because the schedule sits in a different place in each: a backup_entry has no time_window at all - every one of its jobs carries its own - while a restore_entry carries one directly.

Every field carries BOTH 'range_text' (for a person) and 'constraint' (for a program): kind, nullable, min, max, enum, special_values. Prose cannot be checked, and the reason this is data rather than more docs is that a program holds the estate to it: 'python -m db_ops.common.cli check-objects' reads every record at every path in 'used_in' and reports three things - a required field missing, a value out of range, and a field the reference does not describe.

'open_enum': true means an unlisted value is REPORTED, not refused, because the estate may legitimately define its own (a Telegram level, a shell). 'forbidden_in_config': true is the opposite - a field that is valid in an ad-hoc request and must never appear in a config file, because configuration names a secret and does not hold one. 'legacy_fields' are older spellings the parser still reads: present in a file they are reported as deprecated rather than unknown.

It describes; it does not decide. No parser, scheduler or validator reads it, and editing it changes nothing an app does. What earns it its place in data/ is that it cannot go stale: tests/test_shared_config_objects_reference.py checks it against the code AND runs check-objects over this estate's own files, so a field added to lib and not here fails the suite.

EVERY interval in every one of these objects is measured from the previous run's START, never from when it finished. repeat_interval: 300 on a task that runs for 240 seconds starts again about 60 seconds after it ends (45, with the early-start grace). That was not true before 2026-09-19: sql_tasks measured from sql_runs.finished_at and the reports app from the moment its last send completed, so one estate ran three meanings of one field. There is now one entry point, db_ops.lib.time_window.due_from_row, and one place that picks the column, db_ops.lib.time_window.run_anchor.

Wall-clock bounds (from_hour, to_day, ...) are read in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone), and elapsed-time arithmetic is always UTC. The two are different questions and the split is deliberate: see docs/configuration.md section 5.
'why is this not running' is answered by the same rule the schedulers use, without guessing: python -m db_ops.common.cli due-check @data/<request>.json

THREE COPIES, identical bytes: db_ops/common/catalogue/ (the seed init writes from), data/ (this node's), and data/*.example.json (what the public tree ships). Edit one and copy it over the other two; the suite fails if they differ, because reference that differs per node is not reference.

used_in.note: on the JOB, not on the entry: one backup id can have a full and a log job with different schedules and retentions

fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: First calendar year the schedule is allowed in.

fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)

fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: First month of the year the schedule is allowed in.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: Last month. from 11 to 2 is the winter.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: First day OF THE MONTH. There is no weekday dimension: 'weekends only' cannot be said here.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: Last day of the month.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: First hour of the day. The field the estate actually schedules by, and the one whose meaning moves with the node's timezone.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: Last hour. 23 is the idiom for 'all day'; 0 means midnight alone, which is how a schedule fires once a day by accident.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: First minute of the hour. Narrows an hour window; it does not pin a run to a minute, because due-ness is still repeat_interval elapsed and the scheduler only looks on its own sweep.

fields.measured_against: wall clock in the node's configured timezone (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: inclusive; null = no restriction on this dimension; from_ > to_ wraps (22 -> 6 spans midnight)
fields.purpose: Last minute of the hour.

fields.default: null = the app's own default (sql_tasks and reports 300, backup_restore its DEFAULT_REPEAT_SECONDS)
fields.range_text: -1, 0, or 1 and up (seconds), or null. Below -1 is refused

special_values.-1: manual only: never scheduled, forced runs only

fields.rule: a run may start up to min(interval*0.05, 30) seconds early so a sweep boundary does not cost a whole cycle, which is why 1800 is observed as ~1770
fields.purpose: Seconds between STARTS after a run that did not fail. 300 with a task that takes 240 means the next start is about 60 seconds after it finishes - 45 in fact, because of the grace in the rule above.

fields.default: null = the app's own default: daemon 60, metrics 600, sql_tasks and backup_restore fall back to repeat_interval
fields.range_text: 0 and up (seconds), or null. 0 = retry on the next sweep
fields.rule: it can only bring a retry FORWARD, never postpone one: the rule checks 'still running', then 'repeat_interval elapsed', then 'failed', so a failed run is due the moment repeat_interval elapses whatever this says - and a retry_interval LARGER than repeat_interval therefore does nothing at all
fields.purpose: Seconds between starts after a run that ended in error/timeout/fail/failed/failure. Set it BELOW repeat_interval to retry a failure sooner than the normal schedule.

fields.range_text: 0 and up (seconds), or null. 0 = never killed

special_values.0: never killed, for something meant to stay up

fields.rule: also the grace on a 'running' row: a row still open after timeout is reaped instead of a second copy being started
fields.purpose: Seconds a run may take before it is killed. Set it above the SLOWEST thing inside the command and below repeat_interval.

fields.default: null = no restriction, the record may run on any day
fields.range_text: an array of ISO weekdays 1-7 (1=Monday .. 7=Sunday); [] = never runs

special_values.[]: no day is permitted - the record never runs on a schedule
special_values.null: no restriction on the day of the week

fields.measured_against: the day of the week on the node's configured clock (config.json -> timezone)
fields.rule: ISO 1-7, the same numbering isoweekday() and 'date +%u' use, so a config value, DB_OPS_WEEKDAY and a shell script all mean the same thing by 7. 0 is REFUSED rather than dropped: it is the cron spelling of Sunday, and a dropped [0] would become [], which means never. A duplicate is refused too - it is a set, not a weighting. IT GATES DUE-NESS AND DOES NOT GRANT IT: repeat_interval still decides whether, this decides whether today, so a weekly full is weekdays [7] plus an hour window plus an interval WELL UNDER A DAY - with a 6-day interval the due moment walks and the record skips whole weeks. Checked before the five bounds, because a day that is not permitted excludes every hour in it
fields.purpose: Which days of the week the record may run on. The one field that is a SET rather than a from_/to_ pair, because a pair cannot say 'Monday and Thursday'.

reached through notify, so check-objects does not walk it on its own

fields.rule: result sets with the same columns are merged into one table first, so a task that runs once per batch delivers one table. xlsx and xml hold one table; txt, csv and json hold every shape
fields.purpose: none = status only. plain = the rows pasted into messages (~30 rows each). The rest = ONE file sent as one Telegram document - the quiet choice for a result longer than a few dozen rows.

fields.range_text: a routing level such as sql, logging, warning, or ""
fields.rule: looked up in the level -> chat map, like notify_rule.telegram_chat

fields.rule: wins over the level lookup
fields.purpose: One specific chat, for the rare case that needs one. Prefer telegram_chat.

fields.rule: out of range is refused, never clamped
fields.purpose: How many rows plain output fetches and pastes. A file format is not limited by it.

shared_config_objects.one_line: How to reach a HOST's operating system - the block metrics and host_ops read.

not_a_field.platform: Read from the INSTANCE (or inferred from its os text) and written into the resolved block. Inside cmd_access it is ignored, which is worth stating because putting it there looks like it works.

fields.rule: a disabled block needs no credential and is never validated
fields.purpose: Whether db_ops may reach this host's OS at all.

fields.rule: local means INSIDE the db_ops container. With a remote host it reports the container's own CPU and disk under that host's name, so remote_exec refuses the combination
fields.purpose: How a command reaches the host.
Where to connect.

fields.rule: the port the METHOD implies, not the session's
fields.purpose: Which port to connect to.

constraint.open_enum_reason: the value is passed to the host, which may have a shell this list does not know

fields.purpose: Which shell the command text is written for.

fields.rule: ssh only, and the default is the trap: a host reached with a password needs this stated or the login is never attempted
fields.purpose: How the SSH session authenticates.

fields.range_text: a path on the node, or ""
fields.rule: ssh with auth_type key only
fields.purpose: A private key other than the node's own.

fields.rule: winrm only
fields.purpose: Whether WinRM is spoken over HTTPS.

fields.default: "" - but required for winrm, and for ssh with auth_type password
fields.rule: naming an entry wins over any login stated inline: it is asking for THAT entry
fields.purpose: Which stored OS login to use.

fields.rule: with password or password_ref it makes the block self-contained, which is what lets run-cmd reach a host in no inventory
fields.purpose: An inline OS login, instead of a stored one.

fields.range_text: the password itself - and NEVER in a data/*.json

constraint.forbidden_reason: configuration names a secret, it does not hold one; this field is for a request object handed to run-cmd

fields.rule: check-objects reports it as a violation when it appears in a config file
fields.purpose: An inline password, for an ad-hoc request.

fields.range_text: a name in the encrypted secret store, or ""

fields.rule: api and subprocess both mean 'this target's SQL cannot go through a normal driver' (the Oracle 8i bridge); an absent or empty block IS direct, which is what the overwhelming majority of targets say
fields.purpose: How SQL reaches this database.

fields.default: none - required when method is api
fields.rule: refused at load time when method is api and this is blank
fields.purpose: Where the legacy bridge listens.

fields.rule: wins over the credential's own declaration; empty means the credential decides (common.oracle_bridge.connect_mode)
fields.purpose: Which Oracle connect mode the legacy bridge logs in with.

fields.rule: this is the STATEMENT timeout for a legacy target, unrelated to time_window.timeout, which bounds the whole run
fields.purpose: How long one statement may take through the bridge or the subprocess tool.

fields.range_text: a name in the encrypted secret store, or ""
fields.rule: check-credentials and check-secret read this, which they did not until it was written down: a bridge token an estate had configured was invisible to both
fields.purpose: The shared secret the bridge token is signed with.

fields.range_text: a name in the encrypted secret store, or ""
fields.purpose: A whole user/password@host/service connect string, stored as one secret.

shared_config_objects.one_line: How long a directory of backups keeps them, in SECONDS, spelled one way.

used_in.note: on the JOB, not on the entry: one backup id can have a full and a log job with different schedules and retentions

fields.default: none - stating it IS the point. 691200 (8 days) is the recommended value
fields.rule: 0 = no age gate, which is NOT 'keep everything': every file becomes a candidate and the chain rule alone decides (never the newest full, nor anything at or after it). Believing the opposite let a staging directory reach 16.7 GB
fields.purpose: How long a directory of backups keeps them. A backup job prunes its own output; a restore entry prunes the copies it staged.

fields.rule: LEGACY spelling, read but never written. Use cleanup_retention
fields.purpose: What a restore entry used to call cleanup_retention.

fields.range_text: 0 and up, in DAYS (converted, not guessed at)
fields.rule: LEGACY spelling, read but never written. Use cleanup_retention
fields.purpose: What a backup job used to call cleanup_retention.

shared_config_objects.one_line: One scheduled process the daemon runs: what it is, where it runs, when, and how many at once.
shared_config_objects.kind_note: kind is 'field' and not 'record', because that is what the reader does with it: check_data_dir treats a 'field' entry as names living directly ON the record, which is exactly an app command. A 'record' kind would make it look for a nested block called app_command, find none, and certify clean for ever - so do not invent one.

used_in.note: the whole record, not a block inside it. One per scheduled process; the daemon keys them by app_command_id, so a duplicate id keeps only the last record

fields.range_text: any non-empty string; unique across the file
fields.purpose: The identity of this scheduled process. It is the job_code the store records runs under, so renaming one starts a new history and orphans the old rows.
fields.rule: Must be unique: load_app_commands builds a dict keyed by it, so a duplicate id keeps only the LAST record and says nothing about the one it dropped

fields.purpose: The order records are written in when a file is rebuilt from store rows (db/config_store.py).
fields.rule: READ BY NOTHING AT RUN TIME. It does not order execution, does not set priority and does not affect scheduling - the daemon starts whatever is due. Named here because a number that looks like a priority and is not is worth naming

fields.purpose: A short code for the app this command belongs to, so several commands of one app group.
The app's own name, as the logs and the console show it.
What a person reads in Telegram and on the console: a sentence saying what this does.
fields.rule: The legacy spelling command_name is still read and must not be written

fields.default: none - logging refuses an empty scope
fields.purpose: Which log file this command's lines go to, so one app's output is one file.
fields.rule: Validated by db_ops.logging_ops.writer.validate_log_scope, which RAISES on an empty value or a path separator - the one field of the fourteen that can stop the daemon loading the file at all

fields.range_text: a path, or the logical alias tools/db_ops
fields.purpose: Where command_text is run from.
fields.rule: tools/db_ops is a LOGICAL ALIAS for the tool root, not a filesystem path: the image lays the project out under /app/tools/db_ops and the daemon resolves the alias to wherever the project actually lives (db_ops/jobs/daemon.py). Docs printing it as a path are stale

fields.range_text: a command line for the node's own shell
fields.purpose: The process the daemon starts.
fields.rule: It goes through the platform's shell, so SINGLE-QUOTED JSON BREAKS ON WINDOWS - a command passing a JSON request uses @data/<file>.json. Never put a secret here: the file is committed and the line is logged

fields.purpose: Whether the daemon schedules this command at all.
fields.rule: false is how a command is stopped. It is NOT max_parallel 0, which would leave the command due for ever and never run it

fields.purpose: Which node runs this command, matched against DB_OPS_NODE_ROLE at run time.
fields.rule: The shipped catalogue says all, so a single-node install runs everything; this estate's own file says worker because the worker is its scheduler. A node whose role matches nothing runs nothing and reports no error

fields.purpose: Whether the daemon waits for one run to finish before starting the next.
fields.rule: async starts the command whenever it is due, in flight or not - SAFE ONLY IF THE APP REFUSES ITS OWN DUPLICATE WORK through the store claim (ux_sql_runs_claim, ux_job_runs_claim). Declaring async on an app with no claim runs the same unit of work twice. sync is the default and is exactly what every command did before the field existed

fields.default: 4 when run_mode is async and it is unstated; 1 when sync
fields.purpose: How many processes of this one command may be alive at once.
fields.rule: A BRAKE, not a tuning knob: APP-SQL_TASKS is due every second, so without a cap async means a new process every second for as long as the first one runs. REFUSED on a sync command unless it is 1, and refused above 32 - the cost lands on the database being worked, not on this host

fields.default: from_day 1, to_day 31, from_hour 0, to_hour 23, retry_interval 60, timeout 300 - applied by load_app_commands, not by lib/time_window
fields.range_text: a time_window object; see that entry for all of its fields

constraint.checked_by: time_window's own entry, whose used_in already lists app_commands.json:app_commands[]. Declared here as a non-recursing kind so one mistake is not reported twice

fields.measured_against: the previous run's START; the bounds are read in the configured timezone
fields.rule: THIS INTERVAL IS A FLOOR UNDER EVERY UNIT OF WORK INSIDE THE APP. The app is one process working through its own due list, so a task or job declaring 900 s inside an app command declaring 300 s runs every 900-1200 s and nothing in the inner record says why. APP-SQL_TASKS and APP-TELEGRAM use 1 for this reason; APP-BACKUP-RESTORE moved 300 -> 30 on 2026-09-21
fields.purpose: When this command may run, how often, and how long it may take.

fields.range_text: free text, ENGLISH - it is read back through Telegram and the console
fields.purpose: Why this command is configured the way it is.
fields.rule: Say WHY, not what: what a reader needs is the failure that motivated the setting. The shipped catalogue carries one per command explaining the default; an estate file carries one where it differs from that default

shared_config_objects.one_line: One machine's backup registration in restore_config.json -> backup_restore.backups: what to back up and where to put it. It carries NO schedule of its own.
shared_config_objects.kind_note: kind is 'field' for the reason app_command is: check_data_dir reads a 'field' entry as names living directly ON the record, which is what these are. A 'record' kind would look for a nested block called backup_entry, find none, and certify clean for ever.

used_in.note: the whole record, not a block inside it. One per MACHINE's backup set; its jobs[] carry the schedules, so this record has no time_window of its own

fields.purpose: How this registration is addressed: --backup-id, /spbot_backup, and every job_runs row.
fields.rule: It names a MACHINE's backup set, not a database. One entry can cover every database MSSQL_DATABASES lists, which is why a full/diff/log count per ENTRY hides a database with no full of its own

fields.default: none - there is no default machine
fields.purpose: Which machine the job is shipped to, and where its cmd_access and credentials come from.
fields.rule: Checked by check-references. A backup names its machine ONE way, by server_id; a restore_entry names it two, which is the asymmetry the 0.21.0 audit measured

fields.purpose: Which engine's scripts run. It selects the script, not the connection.
fields.rule: Narrower than KNOWN_DB_TYPES (mysql has no backup script) and wider than SQL_TASK_DB_TYPES (what a scheduled SQL task can run on). The three sets are deliberately different, each derived from what its own layer supports

fields.default: none - stating where the pieces go IS the registration
fields.purpose: Where the pieces are written: inside the container when the job sets DOCKER_CONTAINER, on the host otherwise.
fields.rule: Two entries sharing one directory is safe for Oracle (every RMAN FORMAT carries %d) and for SQL Server (the path carries the database name); for PostgreSQL it is made safe by comparing the parent's System-Identifier before an incremental chains onto it

fields.default: none - an entry with no jobs backs nothing up
fields.purpose: The work this registration does. Each element is a backup_job with its OWN schedule.
fields.rule: This is where the schedule lives, and it is the most confusable thing in this file: a backup entry has no time_window, a restore_entry has one. 'the weekly full on Sunday' is weekdays [7] on ONE job beside a sibling pinning the incremental level on the other six days

fields.purpose: Values passed to the script through the environment that must not be written down, resolved from the encrypted store at run time.
fields.rule: BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_PASSWORD belongs here and never in a job's env, which is plain config read back through Telegram

fields.purpose: Whether this registration is scheduled at all.
fields.rule: false stops every job inside it whatever their own flags say. It is also how an entry is held on a master that must not run it: deploy gives the master a shared key, so a master saying false switches it off on the worker - 'master keeps ... STOPS A JOB THAT IS ACTIVE ON THE WORKER' is the line that says so

fields.purpose: Why this record is as it is.
fields.rule: English, like every other note field: these are read back through Telegram

shared_config_objects.one_line: One scheduled piece of work inside a backup_entry's jobs[]: a level, a script, and the schedule that decides when it runs. THE SCHEDULE LIVES HERE, not on the entry.
shared_config_objects.kind_note: kind is 'field': its names live directly on each element of jobs[].

used_in.note: the whole record. THIS is where a backup's schedule lives - the level, the hours and, since 0.21.0, the days

fields.default: none - it selects the script and decides whether a level applies
fields.range_text: database | database_full | wal | archivelog | full | diff | log
fields.purpose: Which shape of work this is. It selects the script and decides whether a level applies at all.
fields.rule: A wal/archivelog/log job has no full-vs-diff level, so --backup-type is refused on one. Two jobs differing only in level and weekdays is how a weekly full sits beside a daily incremental

fields.default: none - the engine's default script for this job type
fields.purpose: The script shipped to the machine and run there.
fields.rule: Resolved through the tool root, so it is the same string on every node

fields.default: empty - the script's own defaults apply
fields.purpose: What the script is told: the level, which databases, which container, which port or SID.
fields.rule: BACKUP_LEVEL states the level and is the JOB's decision, never the script's - a weekday literal inside a script reads the container HOST's clock while its window is read on the node's, which cost five nights on 2026-09-19. DOCKER_CONTAINER is optional since 0.21.0: unset means the engine is on the host. PG_PORT, ORACLE_SID, ORACLE_OS_USER and RMAN_CONFIGURE are the rest, all defaulting to today's behaviour. Nothing secret: use the entry's env_secrets

fields.purpose: When this job runs: the hours, the interval, and since 0.21.0 the days.
fields.rule: weekdays gates due-ness without granting it, so repeat_interval must stay well under a day on a weekday-gated job or the due moment walks out of the window and skips whole cycles. Measured: a full job at repeat_interval 72000 against a four-hour window drifts through it

fields.purpose: How long this job's output is kept.
fields.rule: Seconds, as everywhere it appears. RETENTION_DAYS in env is the SCRIPT's own separate knob and is days

fields.purpose: Which chat hears about this job, per level.
fields.rule: Parsed once in db_ops/lib/notify.py; a per-app copy is a bug

fields.purpose: Whether this one job is scheduled.
fields.rule: Independent of the entry's own active and ANDed with it: turning one level off leaves its siblings running

fields.purpose: Why this record is as it is.
fields.rule: English, like every other note field: these are read back through Telegram

shared_config_objects.one_line: One restore drill in restore_config.json -> backup_restore.restores: which backup to take, which machine to put it on, and when. It carries its schedule DIRECTLY, unlike a backup_entry.
shared_config_objects.kind_note: kind is 'field': its names live directly on the record.

used_in.note: the whole record. Unlike a backup_entry it carries its time_window DIRECTLY, which is the asymmetry these three descriptions exist to make impossible to get wrong

fields.purpose: How this drill is addressed.
fields.rule: Separate from any backup_id: a drill may restore a set taken by another tool entirely

fields.default: none - absent on a script-driven restore
fields.range_text: where the backup is read FROM
fields.purpose: The machine and directory the pieces are copied from.
fields.rule: Nine of the fourteen restores in this estate are script-driven and give script/backup_dir with NO source or target. Both forms are valid, and a registrar that refused the script form shipped in 0.17.0

fields.default: none - absent on a script-driven restore, which is nine of fourteen here
fields.range_text: where the backup is restored TO
fields.purpose: The instance the restore runs against.
fields.rule: The second way a restore names a machine. The 0.21.0 audit measured three target.id values that were ad-hoc labels with an address baked into them, matching nothing in db_instances.json - and found no separate 'ip' field to remove, because the address is inside the label

fields.default: empty - the script decides what it restores
fields.purpose: Which databases this drill restores, and under what names.
fields.rule: A physical restore carries the SOURCE's logins with it, so the target answers to the source's password afterwards and its own stored credential goes stale

fields.purpose: What a report needs to say about the machine without connecting to it.
fields.rule: Descriptive only: nothing schedules or connects from this

fields.purpose: When this drill runs.
fields.rule: DIRECTLY on the entry, which is the difference from a backup_entry - there the window sits on each job. Reading one shape and assuming the other is the mistake these two descriptions exist to prevent

fields.purpose: How long the copied-in pieces are kept on the target.
fields.rule: Seconds. A drill that keeps every copy fills the target host, which killed a daemon 26 minutes into a soak by leaving 42 MB free

fields.purpose: Which chat hears the drill's verdict.
fields.rule: Parsed once in db_ops/lib/notify.py

fields.purpose: Whether this drill is scheduled.
fields.rule: A drill writes to a real instance, so false is the safe state on any node not meant to run it

fields.purpose: Why this record is as it is.
fields.rule: English, like every other note field: these are read back through Telegram
